o.text:
From Proto-Turkic *tik- (“vertical; to plant vertically”).
Compare Turkish dikmek (“to sew”), Kumyk тикмек (tikmek, “to sew; to build”) Kazakh тігу (tigüw).
Ultimately from Latin fōrma, via Russian фо́рма (fórma).
From gəmirmək (“to gnaw”) + -ici. Cognate with Turkish kemirici.
From Arabic دَاخِلِي (dāḵilī). By surface analysis, daxil + -i.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ظَالِم (zalım) (attested in a translation of "Tezkiretü'l-Evliya" in 1341), from Classical Persian ظَالِم (zālim), from Arabic ظَالِم (ẓālim).
Cognate with Turkish zalim, zalım (dialectal, Kırşehir) and Gagauz zulum.
From Persian روحانی, from Arabic رُوحَانِيّ (rūḥāniyy).

Perhaps doublet of dialectal arxanc (“vegetable garden; household plot”), that is arxa (“back [of the house]”) + -(n)c. Final -nc varies regularly with -c, compare e.g. Azerbaijani qılıc~qılınc (“sword”).
Alternatively, from Middle Mongol ᠠᠷᠭᠠᠮᠵᠢ (arɣamǰi); compare Khalkha Mongolian аргамж (argamž, “long rope for tying livestock for keeping to graze around”); Mongolic borrowings: Kyrgyz аргамжы (argamjı), Tajik арғамчин (arġamčin).
Cognate with the synonymous dialectal Turkish arkaç, argaç, arhaç, arḫaç.
Borrowed from Russian гидрография (gidrografija). By surface analysis, hidro- + qrafiya.
